metadata.note: Command teardown of ./art --list and its bare-word alias ./art list. Both share one case branch at art:58-80 (episode.source_sha256 85cf6a0a7a0c3d7b8bd6c2476522102460002fcbbc55b14f55065c46bc244ac1). The middle body reads the actual dispatcher — the case pattern, the 21 printf calls (1 header + 20 skills), the '%-22s %s\n' format string — then a real failure (./art -list exits 2 with a hint on STDOUT, not stderr) and the recovery through ./art <skill> --help. Source grew from 16 to 20 skills between build runs: godot-waikthrough, godot-gamedev, godot-gdd and riff were added; several role descriptions expanded. All demo outputs in demo/RUN-LOG.md are verbatim from this workspace. Playlist adaptation for @HumanitariansAI: composer folder chip reads @HumanitariansAI; outro card is the locked ClaudeTitleOutro with hardcoded @NikBearBrown handle per OUTRO-LOCK.md — flagged for human reviewer before publication. No paid API, no upload.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude UI cold open. Ask lands answered; narration introduces Liam in for Bear.
beats.narration_text: Salaam, this is Liam, in for Bear. Every fellow in Brutalist has typed dot slash art dash dash list at some point. What it does is smaller and more literal than most people think. It prints a hand-typed table of twenty skills. No lookup, no directory scan. Here is exactly what runs, and where it stops.

beats.role_note: FRAMEWORK — the shape of the dispatcher. Two aliases joined by a pipe, one branch.
beats.narration_text: The whole dispatcher is one bash case statement. The second branch of that case is two aliases joined by a pipe: dash dash list and the bare word list. Both hit the same body. You never need to remember which spelling; the case pattern takes both.

show.event: code card fades in with 'art' in the title bar

props.title: art — the dispatcher (bash)
props.code:
case "$cmd" in
  ""|-h|--help|help)
    # …help body…
    ;;
  --list|list)                        # ← two aliases, one branch
    printf '%-22s %s\n' "SKILL" "ROLE"
    printf '%-22s %s\n' "ai-explainer" "builder — …"
    # …nineteen more printf calls…
    ;;
  # …one branch per command…
  *) echo "art: unknown skill '$cmd' (try ./art --list)"; exit 2 ;;
esac

beats.role_note: MECHANISM — the body is 21 printf calls. No directory scan, no plug-in discovery.
beats.narration_text: Here is the body. One printf for the header, then twenty more printfs, one per skill. Every row is a literal string in the file itself. There is no file system scan, no plug-in discovery, no configuration file. If a skill is missing from the table, it is missing because nobody added its printf.

beats.role_note: MECHANISM — the format string is the alignment contract.
beats.narration_text: The format string is worth reading. Percent dash twenty-two s, space, percent s, backslash n. That means: left-pad the first field to twenty-two characters, one space, then the second field, then a newline. Every row is aligned to the same twenty-two-character gutter, which is why the table is scannable without a monospace-aware terminal.

props.title: the format string: '%-22s %s\n'
props.code:
# one printf, the way every row in --list is emitted:
printf '%-22s %s\n' "ai-explainer" "builder — Claude-branded explainer reel (the tight cut)"

# the format string, decomposed:
#   %-22s   → first arg, left-justified, padded to 22 chars
#   ' '     → one literal space (the gutter)
#   %s      → second arg, no padding
#   \n      → one newline

# what the terminal prints for that call:
ai-explainer           builder — Claude-branded explainer reel (the tight cut)
#^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^
# 22 chars              1-space gutter, then the role text runs on.

beats.role_note: MECHANISM — extra arguments are silently ignored. --list is a printer, not a runner.
beats.narration_text: Watch what happens with extra arguments. Dot slash art list foo bar prints the same twenty-one lines and exits zero. The branch never reads the rest of the command line. Compare that to a runner branch like scenes or run, which passes every remaining argument straight to a Python script. List is a printer, not a runner.

# the --list body never references "$@":
--list|list)

    ...

scenes|scene|scene-search)

beats.role_note: FALSIFIABILITY — a real failure. ./art -list (single dash) is NOT an alias; hint lands on STDOUT via bare echo.
beats.narration_text: Now the near miss. Dot slash art dash list, with one dash instead of two, does not print the catalog. It falls into the star branch and exits two, with one hint line pointing you at dash dash list. Notice where that line lands. It is on standard output, from a bare echo. If you pipe standard out to a file, the hint disappears and only the exit code is left behind.

props.title: $ ./art -list  (the failure path)
props.code:
$ ./art -list
art: unknown skill '-list' (try ./art --list)
$ echo $?
2

$ ./art -list 2>/dev/null       # stderr is empty; hint was on stdout
art: unknown skill '-list' (try ./art --list)

$ ./art -list >/dev/null        # pipe stdout — the hint disappears
$ echo $?
2

# From art:127-129 — the catch-all case:
*)
  dir="$(skill_dir "$cmd")"
  [ -z "$dir" ] && { echo "art: unknown skill '$cmd' (try ./art --list)"; exit 2; }
  # …
  ;;
props.sparkLine: Not the catalog. Exit 2. Hint on stdout.

beats.role_note: RECOVERY — two commands cover the whole surface: --list to see, <skill> --help to read.
beats.narration_text: The recovery is two commands. Dot slash art dash dash list to see every skill by name. Then dot slash art followed by the skill name and dash dash help to open that skill's SKILL dot m-d in your pager. So the arc is: list to see what exists, then help on a specific skill to read what it does. Two commands, whole surface.

props.title: wrong guess → recovery in two commands
props.code:
# 1. See every skill (name + one-line role):
$ ./art --list

# 2. Open one skill's SKILL.md in your pager:
$ ./art fellows --help
$ ./art ai-explainer --help
$ ./art nopunt --help

# From art:130-132 — the --help path inside the catch-all:
if [ "${1:-}" = "--help" ] || [ "${1:-}" = "-h" ]; then
  exec "${PAGER:-cat}" "$dir/SKILL.md"
fi

# So the whole surface, two commands:
#   --list                → the catalog
#   <skill> --help        → that skill's SKILL.md

beats.role_note: VERDICT — the split. Lines summarize what --list is and is not.
beats.narration_text: So the split. Art dash dash list is a printer. Two aliases, one branch, a hand-maintained table of twenty skills. Extra arguments are ignored; single dash and unknown tokens exit two with a hint on standard out. The recovery is two commands: dash dash list to see the names, then art followed by a skill name and dash dash help to read what that one does.

props.artifactHeading: art --list vs list vs extras vs unknown token
artifactLines: art --list — a printer of a hand-typed 21-line table (1 header + 20 skills).
art list — the bare-word alias, identical 21-line stdout, exit 0 like --list.
extra positional arguments — silently ignored; the branch never reads "$@".
unknown token like -list or bogus — exit 2, one hint line on stdout (bare echo).
recovery arc — ./art --list to see the names, then ./art <skill> --help to read one.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — Your Turn composer. Prompt read aloud verbatim, then discussed.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude Code from the brutalist toolkit root. Ask it to run both aliases, diff the two outputs, count the rows, then open the case block that produces them and confirm every printf resolves to exactly one row of the printed table. What you should see is two identical outputs of twenty-one lines, twenty printf calls plus a header, and no orphans on either side.
